//| echo: false
transpose = (obj) => {
  if (!obj || Object.keys(obj).length === 0) return [];
  const keys = Object.keys(obj);
  if (keys.length === 0 || !obj[keys[0]]) return [];
  return obj[keys[0]].map((_, i) => {
    const r = {};
    keys.forEach(k => r[k] = obj[k][i]);
    return r;
  });
}
```

## Why This Post Exists

Most of us did not get into research because we love debugging environments, waiting on queues, or fighting invisible data bugs. We got into research because we want to answer hard questions.

Modern scientific work is a software project. Full stop. If your codebase is brittle, your science is brittle. If your workflow is reproducible, your science scales. The degree to which you invest in structure determines whether your future self can trust and extend the work — or will spend a week re-excavating what past-you was thinking.

This post is a practical field guide drawn from a talk I gave on scientific software development in the era of vibecoding: what breaks, what helps, and what I would actually recommend to students trying to do serious technical work in 2026.

---

## Expectation vs. Reality

The biggest mismatch in scientific programming is not about intelligence or domain knowledge. It is about where the time actually goes.

"Conda Hell" is not a joke. It is a tax levied on anyone who did not invest early in environment hygiene. The lesson is not that software is annoying — the lesson is that if you do not invest in structure up front, the friction compounds. Each unresolved environment issue, each manually re-run cell, each figure you cannot reproduce six months later, is a compounding interest payment on technical debt.

---

## A Moral Failure

![](../notebooks/quarto/assets/world_if_meme.jpg){fig-align="center" width="70%"}

The "world if" meme is funny but the underlying point is serious. Enormous amounts of scientific compute have been consumed not on the science but on the scaffolding — re-running lost experiments, porting code that was never meant to be portable, debugging race conditions in ad-hoc parallel scripts. Without SLURM we would have cured cancer by now. (Probably not. But the sentiment captures real frustration.)

The fix is not to heroically tolerate the friction. It is to reduce it structurally.

---

## The Iron Rule

There is a tension every researcher hits:

::: callout
- If you take the time to build software the right way, you worry you will never reuse it.
- If you write sloppy code, it will eventually bite you.
- **Damned if you do. Damned if you don't.**
:::

The way out of this dilemma is a calibrated investment in structure — not gold-plating, not cowboy scripts, but just enough that your future self (or a collaborator) can trust and extend the work.

How much structure is "just enough"? A reasonable heuristic:

![Is It Worth The Time? (XKCD)](../notebooks/quarto/assets/xkcd.jpg){fig-align="center" width="65%"}

If you run a task once a week and automation takes a week to build, it pays for itself in two years. If you run it daily and it takes a day to automate, you break even in a month. Most scientific pipelines fall firmly in the "worth automating" zone.

---

## The Virtuous Cycle of Vibecoding

One underappreciated dynamic in 2026: LLMs and good engineering practices are mutually reinforcing, not in tension.

Good structure — typed interfaces, modular functions, clear config files — makes an LLM a far better collaborator. The LLM can read your Pydantic schema and generate valid configs. It can read your Snakemake rules and extend the pipeline. An unstructured notebook full of global state gives a model nothing useful to reason over.

Conversely, LLMs lower the activation energy for adopting practices that once seemed expensive: writing tests, setting up CI, adding type annotations. The cost-benefit calculation has shifted. A tool that would have taken two days to configure in 2022 can be scaffolded in twenty minutes in 2026.

## The Workflow You Are Actually Building

Before diving into specific tools, it helps to be explicit about the shape of the problem:

::: callout
**The Process**

- You have data or simulation parameters.
- You have a model — ABM, statistical, or ML.
- You want to run sweeps over parameter space with fixed logic.
- You want to collect and visualize results without manual copy-paste.
- You want to turn plots into a publication or shareable artifact.
:::

::: callout-teal
**The Goal**

Automate the plumbing so you can focus on the science. Every hour spent hand-managing results is an hour not spent thinking about what those results mean.
:::

## The Stack at a Glance

Each layer of the pipeline maps to a tool with a clear job:

| Problem | Tooling Choice |
|---|---|
| Reproducible environment | `uv` + lockfiles |
| Data validation | Pydantic schemas |
| Hardware acceleration | PyTorch / JAX |
| Code reliability | Pytest + CI |
| Workflow automation | Snakemake |
| Experiment tracking | Weights & Biases |
| Publication and dashboards | Quarto |

This is not the only valid stack. It is one coherent stack where every tool has a clear job and the tools compose cleanly. Glue code is the enemy — every shell script that bridges two incompatible conventions is a liability.

---

## The Foundation

### 1. Keep Core Logic in Python Source

Notebooks are excellent for exploration. They are poor as the only source of truth for production logic. If your model or simulation lives only in a `.ipynb`, it is not testable, not importable, and nearly impossible to version cleanly.

The pattern: write core logic in `.py` files in a `src/` directory, import it into notebooks for exploration, and import it into scripts for batch runs.

```python
# src/core/model.py — importable, testable, versionable
def simulate_trajectories(
    n_agents: int,
    time_steps: int,
    params: dict[str, float],
) -> list:
    """Simulates N trajectories over T steps."""
    ...
```

Type annotations are not just documentation. They are the interface contract between components, and what let a static analysis tool — or an LLM — reason about your code accurately.

Also: use Git branches and pull requests. Always. Even if you are working alone. A PR is a forcing function for reviewing your own work before merging it.

### 2. Reproducible Environments with `uv`

`uv` is significantly faster than conda and produces exact lockfiles that make environments reproducible across machines — including HPC clusters.

```toml
# pyproject.toml
[project]
name = "scientific_dev"
requires-python = ">=3.12"
dependencies = [
    "jax>=0.9.0",
    "snakemake>=8.4.0",
    "pydantic>=2.12.5",
]
```

Key properties: **speed** (much faster than conda for installs), **exact reproducibility** (`uv.lock` pins every transitive dependency), and **linked dependencies** (prevents identical binaries from being duplicated across environments, which matters when HPC disk quotas are tight).

### 3. Hardware Acceleration with JAX / PyTorch

The rule of thumb: if your computation can be expressed as vectorized operations over arrays, it will run faster on a GPU. The jump in throughput for embarrassingly parallel workloads — parameter sweeps, ensemble simulations, batch inference — is typically one to two orders of magnitude.

JAX is particularly well-suited to scientific computing: it supports automatic differentiation through arbitrary programs (including ODE solvers and agent-based models), and `vmap` turns a function over one data point into a function over a batch with no manual batching logic:

```python
import jax.numpy as jnp
from jax import vmap

def compute_score(x):
    return jnp.sum(jnp.sin(x) ** 2)

# Run over all rows of large_input_matrix in parallel on GPU
batch_score = vmap(compute_score)
scores = batch_score(large_input_matrix)
```

With JAX you can often just swap `np` for `jnp` and get immediate hardware acceleration on the same code. PyTorch is the default for neural networks. For custom simulations or differentiable physics, JAX is usually the better fit.

### 4. Validation with Pydantic

Ad-hoc config dictionaries are a silent source of bugs. A typo in a key, a float where an int is expected, a missing required field — all of these can propagate deep into a run before surfacing. Pydantic catches them at construction time.

```python
# src/core/schema.py
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field, field_validator

class NLPModelConfig(BaseModel):
    model_name: str = Field(default="distilbert-base-uncased")
    adapter_dim: int = Field(default=256)

    @field_validator("adapter_dim")
    def validate_adapter_dim(cls, v: int):
        if v <= 0:
            raise ValueError("adapter_dim must be positive")
        return v
```

Validated schemas have a second benefit in 2026: LLMs can read a Pydantic model and generate valid configurations, test fixtures, and accurate documentation without guessing at the types. Structured code is LLM-legible code.

[View Schema →](https://github.com/WillHWThompson/PythonForScientificDevelopment/blob/main/src/core/schema.py)

## The Plumbing

### 1. Command Center with `just`

`just` is a command runner that acts as a project-wide vocabulary of tasks. Instead of each collaborator remembering the exact flags for `snakemake` or `quarto`, they run `just all` or `just preview`. It enforces that everyone runs tasks in the same environment with the same options.

```make
# Run the full pipeline (local profile, baseline config)
all p="local" c="configs/nlp_baseline.yaml":
    uv run snakemake --workflow-profile ./workflow/profiles/{{p}} --configfile {{c}}

# Preview the Quarto site locally
preview:
    cd notebooks/quarto && quarto preview . --no-browser
```

[View Justfile →](https://github.com/WillHWThompson/PythonForScientificDevelopment/blob/main/justfile)

### 2. Orchestration with Snakemake

Snakemake is a workflow manager that automatically determines what needs to run based on what already exists. If a model checkpoint is present, it skips training and goes straight to evaluation. If you add a new config, it runs only the missing experiments. This "amnesia-proof" property is critical for large sweeps where some runs succeed and others fail.

It also integrates natively with SLURM — the same workflow definition runs locally and on the cluster, with only the profile changing.

```python
# workflow/rules/train.smk
rule train_bert_classifier:
    output:
        weights = "results/{cfg_name}/{params_path}/model.pt",
        stats   = "results/{cfg_name}/{params_path}/training_stats.parquet"
    resources:
        gpu = 1
    shell:
        "PYTHONPATH=src python scripts/run_training.py "
        "--config configs/{wildcards.cfg_name}.yaml "
        "--output {output.weights}"
```

[View Full Rule →](https://github.com/WillHWThompson/PythonForScientificDevelopment/blob/main/workflow/rules/train.smk)

### 3. Testing and CI

A test suite is not bureaucracy. It is the thing that tells you, in thirty seconds, whether the change you just made broke something downstream. For scientific code, the most valuable tests are often integration tests that check the full pipeline on a small synthetic dataset.

```python
# tests/test_nlp_logic.py
def test_validation():
    with pytest.raises(ValueError):
        NLPModelConfig(adapter_dim=-1)
```

CI runs those tests on every push, so breakage surfaces in the branch — not in the final writeup week.

```yaml
# .github/workflows/ci.yml
jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - run: uv run pytest tests/
```

[View CI Workflow →](https://github.com/WillHWThompson/PythonForScientificDevelopment/blob/main/.github/workflows/ci.yml)

### 4. Experiment Tracking with WandB

Once sweeps exceed more than a handful of runs, you need somewhere to store metrics that is not a directory of CSV files. WandB logs metrics in real time, versions every run, and makes it trivial to compare runs across dimensions.

```python
# src/core/trainer.py
def init_logger(self):
    wandb.init(
        project="neural-adapter-research",
        config=self.config.model_dump(),
        name=self.config.full_run_name,
    )

wandb.log({
    "train/step_loss": loss.item(),
    "train/learning_rate": self.optimizer.param_groups[0]["lr"],
    "train/global_step": epoch * len(self.train_loader) + step,
})
```

The `config=self.config.model_dump()` pattern is where Pydantic and WandB meet: every hyperparameter is automatically logged without manual bookkeeping, and every run is reproducible because the config is versioned alongside the weights.

[View Trainer →](https://github.com/WillHWThompson/PythonForScientificDevelopment/blob/main/src/core/trainer.py)

### 5. Storage and Querying with Parquet + DuckDB

Parquet files are the right format for scientific results: columnar, compressed, and queryable with SQL via DuckDB without loading everything into memory. DuckDB's glob syntax lets you query entire result directories as if they were a single table:

```sql
SELECT s.*, m."test/auroc"
FROM read_parquet('results/**/training_stats.parquet') s
LEFT JOIN read_parquet('results/**/test_metrics.parquet') m
  ON s.full_run_name = m.full_run_name
```

For projects with more relational structure, SQLModel provides a type-safe Python ORM. For data-intensive projects on shared infrastructure, UVM's [MYDB](https://webdb.uvm.edu) hosts a MySQL server accessible without setup.

The cell below wires a live DuckDB client to whatever results are on disk. Type arbitrary SQL to explore sweep results without leaving the document.

import pandas as pd
from pathlib import Path

try:
    import duckdb
    con = duckdb.connect()
    files = list(Path("../notebooks/quarto/results").glob("**/training_stats.parquet"))
    if files:
        all_results = con.execute("""
            SELECT s.*, m."test/auroc"
            FROM read_parquet('../notebooks/quarto/results/**/training_stats.parquet') s

    else:
        all_results = pd.DataFrame(columns=["epoch","train_loss","val_loss","accuracy","full_run_name","test/auroc"])
except Exception:
    all_results = pd.DataFrame(columns=["error"])

## Why Quarto Matters

Quarto is not just a rendering tool. It is the integration layer where analysis, narrative, equations, and interactivity can live in one reproducible artifact.

The typical alternative is a patchwork: a Jupyter notebook for analysis, a separate LaTeX file for the paper, figures exported manually and embedded as static images. Every time results change, you update three things and hope they stay in sync. Quarto collapses this into one source of truth.

It also supports multiple output formats from the same source file — HTML, PDF, revealjs slides — which matters when you need to hand the same content to a conference, a collaborator, and a journal.

```markdown

## AI Tools for Students

Two categories worth calling out explicitly:

**IDEs with integrated AI assistance:**

- [VSCode](https://code.visualstudio.com) — the standard; integrates with Copilot and Claude
- [Cursor](https://cursor.com/students) — free for students; strong multi-file context
- [Project IDX / Antigravity](https://antigravity.google/) — agent-native workspace

**LLMs as high-context research partners:**

- [Gemini Pro](https://gemini.google/students/) — 2M token context; good for large codebases
- [GitHub Copilot](https://github.com/education) — free for students via GitHub Education
- [Claude Campus](https://claude.com/programs/campus) — available with campus credits

The key word is *partner*, not *replacement*. An LLM cannot tell you whether your experimental design has a confound, whether your loss curve looks right, or whether your evaluation metric is appropriate for your task. Those judgments require domain expertise. What an LLM can do is eliminate the time spent on boilerplate, configuration, and lookup — which, as the pie chart above shows, is a substantial fraction of a researcher's actual hours.

::: callout-teal
Check out [Fitz's Workflow](https://github.com/FWJK1/workflow) for a clean, student-built example of these practices in action.
:::

## A Live Toy Model

Interactive simulations build intuition faster than static plots — and let you probe edge cases without touching code. The simulation below is a Vicsek model: each agent aligns its heading with the local average heading of its neighbors, plus a noise term. Move your mouse over the canvas to attract the swarm. Drag the sliders to watch the order-disorder phase transition in real time.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof settings = Inputs.form({
  N:          Inputs.range([50, 800], {label: "Agent Count",        step: 10,  value: 400}),
  radius:     Inputs.range([10, 150], {label: "Interaction Radius", step: 5,   value: 45}),
  noise:      Inputs.range([0, 1],    {label: "Entropy (Noise)",    step: 0.05,value: 0.15}),
  speed:      Inputs.range([1, 10],   {label: "Velocity",           step: 0.5, value: 4.5}),
  attraction: Inputs.range([0, 5],    {label: "Mouse Attraction",   step: 0.1, value: 2.5})
})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
{
  const width = 780, height = 480;
  const canvas = html`<canvas width="${width}" height="${height}" style="width:100%;height:480px;border-radius:12px;background:#000;cursor:crosshair;box-shadow:0 10px 30px rgba(0,0,0,0.3);"></canvas>`;
  const ctx = canvas.getContext("2d");

  let agents = Array.from({length: settings.N}, () => ({
    x: Math.random() * width, y: Math.random() * height, theta: Math.random() * Math.PI * 2
  }));
  let mouse = {x: -1000, y: -1000};
  canvas.addEventListener("mousemove", e => {
    const r = canvas.getBoundingClientRect();
    mouse.x = (e.clientX - r.left) * (width / r.width);
    mouse.y = (e.clientY - r.top) * (height / r.height);
  });
  canvas.addEventListener("mouseleave", () => { mouse.x = -1000; mouse.y = -1000; });

  function update() {
    if (agents.length !== settings.N) {
      agents = agents.length < settings.N
        ? [...agents, ...Array.from({length: settings.N - agents.length}, () => ({x: Math.random()*width, y: Math.random()*height, theta: Math.random()*Math.PI*2}))]
        : agents.slice(0, settings.N);
    }
    agents = agents.map(a => {
      let ss = 0, sc = 0, ct = 0;
      for (const b of agents) {
        let dx = b.x - a.x, dy = b.y - a.y;
        if (dx > width/2) dx -= width; if (dx < -width/2) dx += width;
        if (dy > height/2) dy -= height; if (dy < -height/2) dy += height;
        if (dx*dx + dy*dy < settings.radius * settings.radius) { ss += Math.sin(b.theta); sc += Math.cos(b.theta); ct++; }
      }
      let avg = Math.atan2(ss / Math.max(ct,1), sc / Math.max(ct,1));
      if (mouse.x > 0) {
        let mdx = mouse.x - a.x, mdy = mouse.y - a.y;
        if (mdx > width/2) mdx -= width; if (mdx < -width/2) mdx += width;
        if (mdy > height/2) mdy -= height; if (mdy < -height/2) mdy += height;
        let diff = Math.atan2(mdy, mdx) - avg;
        while (diff > Math.PI) diff -= Math.PI*2; while (diff < -Math.PI) diff += Math.PI*2;
        avg += diff * (settings.attraction / 10);
      }
      const t = avg + (Math.random() - 0.5) * settings.noise;
      let x = a.x + Math.cos(t) * settings.speed, y = a.y + Math.sin(t) * settings.speed;
      if (x < 0) x += width; if (x >= width) x -= width;
      if (y < 0) y += height; if (y >= height) y -= height;
      return {x, y, theta: t};
    });
  }

  function draw() {
    ctx.fillStyle = "rgba(0,5,15,0.45)";
    ctx.fillRect(0, 0, width, height);
    ctx.lineWidth = 2.5;
    for (const a of agents) {
      const hue = 280 + Math.sin(a.theta) * 45;
      ctx.strokeStyle = `hsla(${hue},85%,65%,0.8)`;
      ctx.beginPath();
      ctx.moveTo(a.x, a.y);
      ctx.lineTo(a.x - Math.cos(a.theta)*12, a.y - Math.sin(a.theta)*12);
      ctx.stroke();
      ctx.fillStyle = `hsla(${hue},95%,75%,1)`;
      ctx.beginPath(); ctx.arc(a.x, a.y, 2.2, 0, Math.PI*2); ctx.fill();
    }
    update();
    requestAnimationFrame(draw);
  }
  requestAnimationFrame(draw);
  return canvas;
}
```

The order-disorder transition in the Vicsek model is a genuine phase transition: below a critical noise threshold the system spontaneously coordinates; above it, the agents are incoherent. That is physics intuition embedded in forty lines of JavaScript, running in a browser, inside a document that also contains the analysis and the paper. That is the point.

---

## What I'd Tell a Student

1. **Build one reproducible pipeline end-to-end before optimizing anything.** Optimization on a fragile foundation just makes the fragility faster.
2. **Keep your core logic in modules, not only notebooks.** If you cannot `import` it, you cannot test it. If you cannot test it, you cannot trust it.
3. **Let CI catch failures early rather than during the final writeup.** A failing test at 2pm on a Tuesday is a minor annoyance. The same failure the night before submission is a crisis.
4. **Use LLMs as force multipliers, not as replacements for scientific judgment.** They are excellent at boilerplate, configuration, and lookup. They cannot tell you whether your experimental design is valid.

---

## Closing

We are a few years — maybe less — until these tools turn substantially more autonomous. The question is not whether to adopt them, but whether the codebase you eventually hand to a more capable agent is something it can work with.

Brittle notebooks, implicit state, hard-coded paths, and untested logic are not just inconvenient for human collaborators. They are opaque to AI collaborators too. The virtuous cycle only closes if the code is structured well enough for the tool to understand it.

The future is not that AI replaces scientific programming. The future is that scientific programming becomes more ambitious because the fixed costs of good engineering drop. That only works if we still care about validation, reproducibility, and clarity.

Let the tools remove friction. Keep your scientific standards high. And maybe, with the time saved, we can cure cancer after all.

*We have a couple of years until they turn us into paper clips. Let's make the most of it.*
